one_liner: Header-only Padé-polynomial libm replacements for exp/log/trig/asin-acos-atan/isqrt, auto-vectorizable, 1.3-13x faster scalar.
what_it_does: VDT provides inline, header-only replacements for libm's transcendental math functions: exp, log, sin, cos, tan, tanh, asin, acos, atan, atan2, and isqrt (1/sqrt), in double and single precision. Functions live in the vdt:: namespace with fast_ prefixes (vdt::fast_exp, vdt::fast_sinf, vdt::fast_logv for arrays), not as std:: overloads, so call sites must be rewritten explicitly. Every function has a scalar T(T) signature and an array void(unsigned int, T*, T*) signature; an optional PRELOAD CMake build mode can additionally intercept existing libm calls at runtime without touching source.
how_it_is_fast: Each function is a Padé/minimax rational-polynomial approximation adapted from the Cephes math library, evaluated with a small fixed number of multiply-adds instead of libm's argument-reduction-and-table-lookup algorithms. The scalar code uses no intrinsics, so it auto-vectorizes under GCC/Clang/ICC into SSE/AVX/AVX2(+FMA) loops; the array (*_v) signatures make this explicit for the compiler and unlock the larger SIMD gains. Accuracy is deliberately relaxed (~0.1-0.5 average LSB difference from libm per the README's own table) to keep polynomial degree and branching low.
when_to_use: Hot loops calling exp/log/sin/cos/tan/asin/acos/atan/atan2/isqrt millions of times where ~0.1-0.5 ULP error is acceptable, e.g. physics simulation and reconstruction code (VDT originated at CERN and is used in Geant4 and LHC experiment software).
Code that can call the array (*_v) signatures or already auto-vectorizes, since SIMD gains (SSE/AVX/AVX2+FMA) are consistently larger than scalar gains in both the README table and the cited paper.
x86-64 builds where you can pick SSE/AVX/AVX2/FMA at CMake configure time, or ARM builds via the NEON CMake option (though NEON is not exercised in the published benchmarks).
Projects willing to vendor a small LGPL-3 header-only library and either call vdt:: functions directly or use the PRELOAD build to intercept an existing libm-calling binary without recompiling it.
when_not_to_use: Need bit-identical results to libm/std math (finance, reproducibility-critical or correctness-critical code) — VDT trades ~0.1-0.5 ULP accuracy for speed on every function.
Building on Windows: issue #1 (open) reports it isn't compatible (__restrict__ vs __restrict, missing _USE_MATH_DEFINES) with no merged fix.
Building on aarch64: default CMake option SSE=ON still passes -msse and breaks the build (issue #21, filed 2025-04-29, open, unresolved as of the last commit).
Scalar single-precision expf/logf/isqrtf specifically — the record's own benchmark numbers show these particular scalar variants are slower than glibc libm.

Teams that need active upstream support: last commit 2025-04-03, several issues open for years (CMake overwrites user CXX flags, clang linking error, Python 3.12 removed the imp module the Python scripts depend on).

integration.dependencies: none (optional Vc library integration via USE_VC CMake option)
integration.min_toolchain: GCC >=4.8, AppleClang >=5.0, Clang >=3.3, or ICC >=15.0 (enforced by CMakeLists.txt); C++11 is required only to build the optional DIAG benchmarking/unit-test tools, not to use the headers
integration.platforms: x86-64 primarily (SSE on by default, AVX/AVX2/FMA opt-in via CMake flags); NEON is an opt-in CMake option for ARM but the default aarch64 build is currently broken by the SSE flag (issue #21); not Windows-compatible per issue #1
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the scalar functions inspected (exp.h, stdwrap.h) are stateless/pure with no shared mutable state, so concurrent calls appear safe, but no explicit guarantee is stated anywhere in the docs
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — functions are not std:: overloads, callers must explicitly call vdt::fast_* instead of std::exp/std::sin/etc.; only the optional PRELOAD build mode intercepts existing libm calls at runtime without source changes

gotchas: fast_expf has a documented undefined-behavior bug (left shift of a negative value) for large negative inputs such as -163.48, caught by UBSan; open since 2019 (issue #10) with a proposed but unmerged fix.
Default CMake option SSE=ON means a plain `cmake .` still emits -msse even on non-x86 targets, which currently breaks aarch64 builds (issue #21).
Accuracy varies per function: the README's own table shows isqrt averaging ~0.45 LSB off libm, the largest deviation of any function in the library.
CMake overwrites user-supplied CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS instead of appending to them (issue #8, open since 2018).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick VDT over SLEEF or trigno_simd_cpp when you want one small header-only LGPL library covering the whole transcendental family (exp/log/trig/inverse-trig/isqrt) with a production track record in CERN/Geant4 physics code, rather than SLEEF's correctly-rounded (1-ulp) precision or trigno_simd_cpp's narrower sin/cos/tan-only scope; choose SLEEF instead when correct rounding matters more than raw speed.
verified_claims_summary: The refereed CHEP2013 paper (glibc 2.12 libm vs VDT v0.3.6, GCC 4.8.1, Intel Core i7-4770K) reports scalar double-precision speedups from ~1.3x (isqrt) to ~12.8x (exp), with AVX2+FMA-vectorized log reaching ~22x; the README's separate i7-3930K table shows smaller but consistent scalar gains (Exp 2.7x, Log 2.8x, Tan 3.7x) rising to 4-8x with SSE/AVX. Both sources agree that scalar single-precision expf/logf/isqrtf are slower than libm.
status_note: Maintenance is stale (last commit 2025-04-03; multiple issues from 2016-2025 remain open, including a Windows-incompatibility report and an unfixed UB bug), but it's LGPL-3.0-or-later, header-only, and small enough to vendor; it's still cited in the repo description as used in CERN's Geant4 and LHC experiment software.
